claim: Outer hair cells (OHCs) in the mammalian ear exhibit electromotility, electrically driven somatic length changes.
source: Outer hair cells (OHCs) in the mammalian ear exhibit electromotility, electrically driven somatic length changes that are thought to mechanically amplify sound-evoked vibrations.
evidence: This is a well-established scientific fact about OHCs, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: OHC electromotility is thought to mechanically amplify sound-evoked vibrations.
source: Outer hair cells (OHCs) in the mammalian ear exhibit electromotility, electrically driven somatic length changes that are thought to mechanically amplify sound-evoked vibrations.
evidence: This represents the prevailing theory in the field that the authors are testing.

claim: For OHC amplification to work, OHCs must respond to sounds on a cycle-by-cycle basis even at frequencies that exceed the low-pass corner frequency of their cell membranes.
source: For this amplification to work, OHCs must respond to sounds on a cycle-by-cycle basis even at frequencies that exceed the low-pass corner frequency of their cell membranes.
evidence: This is a logical requirement derived from the prevailing theory of OHC function.

claim: OHC vibrations measured in the 13–25 kHz region of the gerbil cochlea were strongly rectified.
source: Using in vivo optical vibrometry we tested this theory by measuring sound-evoked motility in the 13–25 kHz region of the gerbil cochlea. OHC vibrations were strongly rectified
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental measurements reported in the study.

claim: OHC motility exhibited first-order low-pass characteristics with corner frequencies around 3 kHz.
source: OHC vibrations were strongly rectified, and motility exhibited first-order low-pass characteristics with corner frequencies around 3 kHz– more than 2.5 octaves below the frequencies the OHCs are expected to amplify.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The measured OHC corner frequencies are more than 2.5 octaves below the frequencies the OHCs are expected to amplify.
source: OHC vibrations were strongly rectified, and motility exhibited first-order low-pass characteristics with corner frequencies around 3 kHz– more than 2.5 octaves below the frequencies the OHCs are expected to amplify.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between measured corner frequencies and the characteristic frequencies of the recording locations.

claim: OHCs operate more like envelope detectors in a classical gain-control scheme than like high-frequency sound amplifiers.
source: These observations lead us to suggest that the OHCs operate more like the envelope detectors in a classical gain-control scheme than like high-frequency sound amplifiers.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their experimental findings.

claim: Up to a few kilohertz, IHC synapses can phase-lock.
source: Up to a few kilohertz, IHC synapses can 'phase-lock,' that is, code the individual cycles of tones.
evidence: This is established knowledge about inner hair cell function.

claim: At frequencies above 3 kHz, phase-locking rapidly declines in IHCs.
source: At higher frequencies (>3 kHz), phase-locking rapidly declines and neural coding relies on the DC component of the IHC receptor potential generated by the asymmetric, or rectifying, nature of the IHC receptor current (Russell and Sellick, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: At high frequencies, neural coding relies on the DC component of the IHC receptor potential generated by the asymmetric, or rectifying, nature of the IHC receptor current.
source: At higher frequencies (>3 kHz), phase-locking rapidly declines and neural coding relies on the DC component of the IHC receptor potential generated by the asymmetric, or rectifying, nature of the IHC receptor current (Russell and Sellick, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Outer hair cells modify the mechanical vibrations inside the organ of Corti, enabling frequency tuning and dynamic range compression.
source: Outer hair cells (OHC) modify the mechanical vibrations inside the organ of Corti (OoC), enabling frequency tuning and dynamic range compression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about OHC function.

claim: Dysfunctional and missing OHCs strongly reduce sensitivity and are a major cause of sensorineural hearing loss.
source: Dysfunctional and missing OHCs strongly reduce sensitivity, and this is a major cause of sensorineural hearing loss (Ryan and Dallos, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Isolated OHCs exhibit length changes driven by variations in the membrane potential.
source: The discovery of electromotility, length changes of isolated OHCs (Brownell et al., 1985) driven by variations in the membrane potential (Santos-Sacchi and Dilger, 1988), has intensified the study of OHCs and their functional significance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The membrane protein responsible for electromotility has been identified.
source: The membrane protein responsible for electromotility has been identified (Zheng et al., 2000), and prestin knockout mice have profound hearing loss (Liberman et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Prestin knockout mice have profound hearing loss.
source: The membrane protein responsible for electromotility has been identified (Zheng et al., 2000), and prestin knockout mice have profound hearing loss (Liberman et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The dominant view is that OHC electromotility drives vibrations within the OoC in a cycle-by-cycle manner over the entire audible range.
source: The dominant view is that OHC electromotility drives vibrations within the OoC in a cycle-by-cycle manner (Ashmore, 2011) over the entire audible range, which extends up to 150 kHz in some species (Vater and Kössl, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The audible range extends up to 150 kHz in some species.
source: The dominant view is that OHC electromotility drives vibrations within the OoC in a cycle-by-cycle manner (Ashmore, 2011) over the entire audible range, which extends up to 150 kHz in some species (Vater and Kössl, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The membrane capacitance is expected to reduce the AC receptor potentials of OHCs at a rate of 6 dB per octave.
source: If this view is correct, the AC receptor potentials of OHCs must be large enough to be effective up to high frequencies, even though the membrane capacitance is expected to reduce the AC receptor potentials (and hence the OHCs' motility) at a rate of 6 dB per octave (Dallos, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and represents established biophysical principles.

claim: Electrical low-pass filtering limits the OHC's ability to provide cycle-by-cycle mechanical feedback, known as the RC problem.
source: The functional implication of this electrical low-pass filtering is a limitation in the OHC's ability to provide cycle-by-cycle mechanical feedback, known as the RC problem (Ashmore, 2011; Housley and Ashmore, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The electrical corner frequency of OHCs has been measured electrophysiologically in vitro, with highest values ranging from 480 Hz to 1250 Hz.
source: The electrical corner frequency of OHCs has been measured electrophysiologically in vitro, with highest values ranging from 480 Hz (Mammano and Ashmore, 1996) to 1250 Hz (Johnson et al., 2011), but no systematic in vivo data exist due to technical limitations and the cochlea's extreme vulnerability.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: No systematic in vivo data on OHC electrical corner frequency exist due to technical limitations and the cochlea's extreme vulnerability.
source: The electrical corner frequency of OHCs has been measured electrophysiologically in vitro, with highest values ranging from 480 Hz (Mammano and Ashmore, 1996) to 1250 Hz (Johnson et al., 2011), but no systematic in vivo data exist due to technical limitations and the cochlea's extreme vulnerability.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: An early in vitro report claimed a bandwidth for electromotility of at least 79 kHz.
source: An early in vitro report claiming a bandwidth for electromotility of at least 79 kHz (Frank et al., 1999) was recently challenged (Santos-Sacchi and Tan, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The claim of 79 kHz bandwidth for electromotility was recently challenged.
source: An early in vitro report claiming a bandwidth for electromotility of at least 79 kHz (Frank et al., 1999) was recently challenged (Santos-Sacchi and Tan, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In vivo estimates of the corner frequency of motility are missing.
source: Again, in vivo estimates of the corner frequency of motility are missing.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: Vibrations in the OHC/Deiters' cell region showed a strong envelope-following component in response to a tone pair.
source: In response to a tone pair (Figure 1A), vibrations in the OHC/Deiters' cell region showed a strong envelope-following component (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The envelope-following component reveals a significant degree of rectification in OHC motion, producing 2nd-order distortions such as the quadratic difference tone at f2-f1.
source: This reveals a significant degree of rectification in OHC motion, producing 2nd-order distortions (DP2s) such as the 'quadratic difference tone' at f2-f1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed envelope-following component based on nonlinear systems theory.

claim: DP2s were concentrated in the OHC/Deiters' cell hotspot area.
source: Using multitone stimuli, we mapped the spatial profile of the DP2s inside the OoC by cross-section measurements. DP2s were concentrated in the OHC/Deiters' cell 'hotspot area' (Cooper et al., 2018) (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the spatial mapping measurements shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: DP2s were observed at stimulus levels as low as 25 dB SPL.
source: They were observed at stimulus levels as low as 25 dB SPL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and disappeared post mortem (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: DP2s disappeared post mortem.
source: They were observed at stimulus levels as low as 25 dB SPL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and disappeared post mortem (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: OHCs are the source of the DP2s long known to exist from psychophysical, electrophysiological, and cochlear-mechanical studies.
source: These observations confirm that OHCs are the source of the DP2s long known to exist from psychophysical (Zwicker, 1979), electrophysiological (Kim et al., 1980; Nuttall and Dolan, 1993), and cochlear-mechanical (Cooper and Rhode, 1997) studies.
evidence: This is an inference from the current observations combined with citations to prior research.

claim: The OHC origin of DP2s is consistent with the significant rectified ('DC') component and 2nd harmonics observed in in vivo recordings of OHC receptor potentials.
source: The OHC origin of DP2s is consistent with the significant rectified ('DC') component and 2nd harmonics observed in in vivo recordings of OHC receptor potentials (Dallos, 1986; Cody and Russell, 1987) and cochlear microphonics (Gibian and Kim, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rectification by OHC bundles produces DP2s in the receptor current.
source: Because rectification by OHC bundles produces DP2s in the receptor current, DP2s are an inevitable part of the electromotile response.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of electromotility.

claim: DP2s are an inevitable part of the electromotile response.
source: Because rectification by OHC bundles produces DP2s in the receptor current, DP2s are an inevitable part of the electromotile response.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of electromotility.

claim: The DP2 part of the electromotile response can be isolated through spectral analysis from recorded cochlear vibrations.
source: More importantly, this part can be isolated through spectral analysis from recorded cochlear vibrations.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the analysis approach.

claim: The DP2 spectrum is ideally suited to studying the RC problem.
source: This makes the DP2 spectrum ideally suited to studying the RC problem.
evidence: This is the authors' reasoning for their methodological approach.

claim: Rectifying an N-component zwuis stimulus generates N² distinct DP2 components at frequencies fk ±fm.
source: Rectifying an N-component zwuis stimulus generates N2 distinct DP2 components at frequencies fk ±fm, each of which can be traced back to a pair of interacting primary frequencies (fk,fm).
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the zwuis stimulus cited from prior work.

claim: The vibration spectrum obtained in the OHC region evoked by a zwuis stimulus reveals a rich family of DP2s having a systematic 6-dB/octave roll-off.
source: The vibration spectrum obtained in the OHC region (Figure 1F) evoked by this stimulus reveals a rich family of DP2s having a systematic 6-dB/octave roll-off.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The 6-dB/octave roll-off confirms the action of a low-pass filter between the hair bundle's rectification and the motile response.
source: This roll-off confirms the action of a low-pass filter between the hair bundle's rectification and the motile response.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed roll-off based on signal processing theory.

claim: Accurate estimation of the corner frequency is hampered by the ~10-dB scatter of DP2 magnitudes within each frequency band.
source: Accurate estimation of the corner frequency, however, is hampered by the ~10-dB scatter of DP2 magnitudes within each frequency band.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Three causes of scatter in DP2 magnitudes were identified.
source: We identified three causes of this scatter (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the authors' analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: Elimination of the three causes of scatter reduces the scatter substantially.
source: Their elimination reduces the scatter substantially, paving the way to accurate estimates of OHC corner frequencies.
evidence: This is a statement about the effect of the methodological corrections.

claim: When supplying an equal-amplitude input to a rectifier, the resulting second harmonics 2fk are 6 dB below the remaining DP2s.
source: The first cause of scatter is combinatorial: when supplying an equal-amplitude input to a rectifier, the resulting second harmonics 2fk are 6 dB below the remaining DP2s (fk ±fm, k > m) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A and explained by nonlinear systems theory.

claim: The 6-dB difference in second harmonics reflects the binomial coefficients occurring in the second-order terms of the power series describing the nonlinearity.
source: This reflects the binomial coefficients occurring in the second-order terms of the power series describing the nonlinearity (Meenderink and van der Heijden, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and mathematical theory.

claim: The primaries and DP2s propagate as traveling waves.
source: The second cause of scatter is the spatially distributed nature of DP2 generation. The primaries and DP2s propagate as traveling waves (Kim et al., 1980; Gibian and Kim, 1982), (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The recorded DP2s are a vector sum of contributions along the path from stapes to recording place.
source: so the recorded DP2s are a vector sum of contributions along the path from stapes to recording place (Schroeder, 1969)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The magnitude of slowly propagating components is affected by interference across generation loci.
source: The magnitude of slowly propagating components is affected by interference across generation loci (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 2B and is a consequence of wave propagation.

claim: Confounding effects of propagation are eliminated by setting an upper frequency limit to the primaries and DP2s at half the characteristic frequency (CF/2).
source: These confounding effects of propagation are eliminated by setting an upper frequency limit to the primaries and DP2s used for stimulation, analysis and iterated adjustment of the stimulus as described below. For this frequency limit we choose half the characteristic frequency (CF/2).
evidence: This is a methodological decision made by the authors.

claim: Wave propagation below CF/2 is too fast to cause interference.
source: Wave propagation below CF/2 is too fast to cause interference and magnitudes change little during fast propagation (Ren et al., 2011) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Magnitudes change little during fast propagation below CF/2.
source: Wave propagation below CF/2 is too fast to cause interference and magnitudes change little during fast propagation (Ren et al., 2011) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amplitude of a DP2 component is proportional to the product of its parents' amplitudes.
source: The amplitude of a DP2 component is proportional to the product of its parents' amplitudes (van der Heijden and Joris, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and is a property of second-order nonlinearities.

claim: Bilinearity causes a scatter in DP2 magnitude (expressed in decibels) equal to twice the range of the primary input magnitudes.
source: This bilinearity causes a scatter in DP2 magnitude (expressed in decibels) equal to twice the range of the primary input magnitudes (Figure 2C and Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C and Appendix 1—figure 1 and is a mathematical consequence of bilinearity.

claim: The effective OHC input can be retrieved from the rich DP2 spectrum by exploiting the bilinear relationship between primary and DP2 amplitudes.
source: Current in vivo measurement techniques lack the spatial resolution to determine OHC bundle deflection, but the effective OHC input can be retrieved from the rich DP2 spectrum by exploiting the bilinear relationship between primary and DP2 amplitudes.
evidence: This is a methodological approach developed by the authors.

claim: The computational method to retrieve effective OHC input was previously used to retrieve the effective IHC input from auditory-nerve responses.
source: This computational method was previously used to retrieve the effective IHC input from auditory-nerve responses (van der Heijden and Joris, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The OHC input obtained differs from the linear component of OHC motion and resembles basilar membrane motion more closely.
source: The OHC input thus obtained differs from the linear component of OHC motion, and in fact resembles basilar membrane motion more closely (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Motion recorded in the OHC region may not be used as a proxy for OHC input.
source: This means that motion recorded in the OHC region may not be used as a proxy for OHC input.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that OHC input differs from OHC motion.

claim: Experimental equalization of the effective OHC input and compensation for the combinatorial effect markedly reduced the scatter in the DP2 spectrum.
source: Experimental equalization of the effective OHC input and compensation for the combinatorial effect had the predicted effect of markedly reducing the scatter in the DP2 spectrum (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: After equalization, the DP2 spectrum recorded from the OHCs closely resembles that of a simple nonlinear circuit with first-order low-pass characteristics.
source: After equalization, the DP2 spectrum recorded from the OHCs closely resembles that of the simple nonlinear circuit of Figure 2A with its first-order low-pass characteristics.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis comparing experimental results to the model circuit.

claim: The first-order low-pass characteristics hold for both the magnitude and the phase, having a minus 6-dB/octave high-frequency slope and a 0.25-cycle high-frequency asymptote respectively.
source: This holds for both the magnitude and the phase, having a minus 6-dB/octave high-frequency slope and a 0.25-cycle high-frequency asymptote (Figure 4C) respectively.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For the 16-kHz CF recording, the corner frequency was 2.5 kHz, 2.7 octaves below the CF.
source: The corner frequency was 2.5 kHz, 2.7 octaves below the 16-kHz CF.
evidence: This is a specific result from one of the recordings.

claim: Data were obtained from different cochlear regions in different animals, with CFs ranging from 13 to 25 kHz.
source: We obtained data from different cochlear regions in different animals, with CFs ranging from 13 to 25 kHz.
evidence: This describes the experimental dataset.

claim: The adjustment of the relative stimulus amplitudes always reduced the scatter of the DP2 magnitudes.
source: The adjustment of the relative stimulus amplitudes always reduced the scatter of the DP2 magnitudes.
evidence: This is a consistent observation across all recordings.

claim: First-order low-pass characteristics were consistently found across CFs.
source: First-order low-pass characteristics were consistently found across CFs (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary of the results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The corner frequencies obtained ranged from 2.1 to 3.3 kHz.
source: The corner frequencies obtained ranged from 2.1 to 3.3 kHz, showing a weak trend of increasing with CF (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The corner frequencies show a weak trend of increasing with CF.
source: The corner frequencies obtained ranged from 2.1 to 3.3 kHz, showing a weak trend of increasing with CF (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the frequency range probed (below CF/2), stiffness dominates OoC impedance rendering displacement proportional to force.
source: In the frequency range probed here (below CF/2) stiffness dominates OoC impedance rendering displacement proportional to force (Dong and Olson, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Within the framework of models in which OHCs directly push the basilar membrane, electromotile force itself suffers from the 6-dB/octave roll-off.
source: Thus within the framework of models in which OHCs directly push the basilar membrane (e.g., Ramamoorthy et al., 2007), electromotile force itself suffers from the 6-dB/octave roll-off.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that displacement is proportional to force in the frequency range tested.

claim: The corner frequencies of 2.1–3.3 kHz measured in vivo were 2.8 ± 0.2 octaves below the CFs of the recording locations.
source: The corner frequencies of 2.1–3.3 kHz that we measured in vivo were 2.8 ± 0.2 octaves below the CFs of our recording locations.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the experimental results.

claim: The in vivo corner frequencies are higher than values of membrane corner frequency from in vitro studies at lower CF.
source: These corner frequencies are higher than values of membrane corner frequency from in vitro studies at lower CF: 480 Hz (guinea pig, CF ~7 kHz) (Mammano and Ashmore, 1996); 300–1250 Hz (gerbil, CF,~350–2500 Hz) (Johnson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current results and prior in vitro studies.

claim: The in vivo data fall considerably short of the extrapolations to higher CFs made in the in vitro gerbil study.
source: The in vivo data fall considerably short of the extrapolations to higher CFs made in the in vitro gerbil study (Johnson et al., 2011) (which predict electrical corner frequencies of 6.5–11 kHz for the CFs tested here).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current results and predictions from prior research.

claim: The observation of a simple 6-dB/octave roll-off and minus 0.25-cycle phase asymptote indicates the dominance of a single low-pass mechanism in the entire frequency range tested.
source: Our observation of a simple 6-dB/octave roll-off and minus 0.25-cycle phase asymptote indicates the dominance of a single low-pass mechanism in the entire frequency range tested.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed characteristics of the frequency response.

claim: Comparison with the in vitro data suggests that the dominant low-pass factor is the RC time of the cell membrane.
source: Comparison with the in vitro data suggests that this dominant factor is the RC time of the cell membrane, which is fundamental to the operation of all biological cells.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing in vivo and in vitro results.

claim: The RC time of the cell membrane is fundamental to the operation of all biological cells.
source: Comparison with the in vitro data suggests that this dominant factor is the RC time of the cell membrane, which is fundamental to the operation of all biological cells.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: The somewhat higher corner frequencies of the present study (compared to the in vitro data) may be attributed to the more basal location of the OHCs.
source: The somewhat higher corner frequencies of the present study (compared to the in vitro data) may be attributed the more basal location of the OHCs of the present study.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the difference between in vivo and in vitro results.

claim: A corner frequency at 2.8 octaves below CF implies a 17-dB attenuation of the CF component.
source: A corner frequency at 2.8 octaves below CF implies a 17-dB attenuation of the CF component.
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation based on the measured corner frequencies.

claim: The shallow increase of OHC corner frequency with increasing CF suggests an even stronger attenuation at higher CFs than studied here.
source: The shallow increase of OHC corner frequency with increasing CF suggests an even stronger attenuation at higher CFs than studied here.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed trend in corner frequencies.

claim: When driven by a sufficiently large electrical input, OHC motility can generate vibrations up to very high frequencies, both in vitro and in vivo.
source: When driven by a sufficiently large electrical input, OHC motility can generate vibrations up to very high frequencies, both in vitro (Frank et al., 1999) and in vivo (Ren et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For acoustic stimulation, the low-pass filtering of the receptor potential will limit the frequency range of OHC motility.
source: but for acoustic stimulation the low-pass filtering of the receptor potential will limit the frequency range.
evidence: This is an inference from the measured low-pass characteristics.

claim: The findings do not support schemes proposed to push the frequency limit of electromotility beyond the corner frequency of the OHC cell membrane into the CF range.
source: Various schemes (reviewed in Johnson et al., 2011) have been proposed to push the frequency limit of electromotility beyond the corner frequency of the OHC cell membrane into the CF range. Our findings do not support such schemes, as the ~2.5-kHz corner frequency is evident in the motile response itself.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings in relation to prior theories.

claim: A 16-kHz tone at the behavioral threshold of the gerbil is estimated to evoke an AC component of the OHC receptor potential of 5.7 μV at the peak of traveling wave.
source: A 16-kHz tone at the behavioral threshold of the gerbil is estimated to evoke an AC component of the OHC receptor potential of 5.7 μV at the peak of traveling wave.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on calculations described in Appendix 2.

claim: At the slightly more basal location where cycle-by-cycle amplification is assumed to start, the AC component is ~1 μV.
source: At the slightly more basal location where cycle-by-cycle amplification is assumed to start, it is ~1 μV.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on calculations.

claim: Inspection of the in vivo OHC recordings in guinea pig yield a 3.6-μV AC component at CF for a 17-kHz tone near the behavioral threshold.
source: Inspection of the in vivo OHC recordings in guinea pig of Cody and Russell (1987) yield an 3.6-μV AC component at CF for a 17-kHz tone near the behavioral threshold, corresponding to ~0.6 μV at the spatial onset of the putative amplification.
evidence: This is an analysis of data from a prior study.

claim: Even if minute variations in the membrane potential could evoke a significant electromotile response, such a motile feedback is unlikely to improve sensitivity because of its expected poor signal-to-noise ratio.
source: Even if these minute variations in the membrane potential could evoke a significant electromotile response, such a motile feedback is unlikely to improve sensitivity because of its expected poor signal-to-noise ratio (van der Heijden and Versteegh, 2015a).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior work on signal-to-noise considerations.

claim: OHCs and IHCs have similar properties, namely, considerable rectification and a corner frequency not exceeding a few kilohertz.
source: Overall our data suggest that OHCs and IHCs have similar properties, namely, considerable rectification (Pappa et al., 2019) and a corner frequency not exceeding a few kilohertz.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the current findings with prior knowledge about IHCs.

claim: Just like in high-frequency IHCs, the receptor potential of high-frequency OHCs is expected to mainly follow the envelope of the waveform that stimulates their hair bundles.
source: Thus, just like in high-frequency IHCs, the receptor potential of high-frequency OHCs is expected to mainly follow the envelope of the waveform that stimulates their hair bundles.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed low-pass characteristics.

claim: Both IHC and OHCs operate as envelope detectors.
source: In this sense both IHC and OHCs operate as envelope detectors.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed properties of both cell types.

claim: OHC motility does not provide cycle-by-cycle feedback, but rather modulates sound-evoked vibrations.
source: We therefore propose that OHC motility does not provide cycle-by-cycle feedback, but rather modulates sound-evoked vibrations (Cooper et al., 2018; van der Heijden and Versteegh, 2015b).
evidence: This is the authors' proposed interpretation of OHC function based on their findings.

claim: In the proposed scenario, the dynamic range compression in the cochlea is based on an automatic gain control system in which the degree of OHC depolarization determines the gain.
source: In this scenario the dynamic range compression in the cochlea is based on an automatic gain control system (van der Heijden, 2005) in which the degree of OHC depolarization determines the gain.
evidence: This is a proposed model for cochlear function based on the findings.

claim: The spatial confinement of the motile response to the OHC/Deiters' cell region presents a challenge to the prevailing theory that OHCs drive basilar membrane motion directly.
source: The spatial confinement of the motile response to the OHC/Deiters' cell region presents another challenge to the prevailing theory that OHCs drive basilar membrane motion directly.
evidence: This is an inference from the spatial distribution of DP2s observed in the study.

claim: The spatial confinement suggests that electromotility controls the local coupling between OHCs and Deiters' cells in a parametric fashion, perhaps dynamically adjusting the amount of dissipation in the Deiters' cell layer.
source: It rather suggests that electromotility controls the local coupling between OHCs and Deiters' cells in a parametric fashion, perhaps dynamically adjusting the amount of dissipation in the Deiters' cell layer.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the spatial confinement observation.

claim: Sound evoked vibrations were recorded from the ossicles and cochlear partitions of deeply anesthetized female gerbils.
source: Sound evoked vibrations were recorded from the ossicles and cochlear partitions of deeply anesthetized female gerbils (n = 27, weight = 53–75 g).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and procedures.

claim: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) measurements were made from the first turn of the intact cochlea, under open-bulla conditions.
source: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) measurements were made from the first turn of the intact cochlea, under open-bulla conditions – optical access to the partition being provided through the transparent round window membrane.
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: The hearing thresholds of the animals were assayed using tone-evoked compound action potential (CAP) measurements.
source: The hearing thresholds of the animals were assayed using tone-evoked compound action potential (CAP) measurements from a silver electrode placed on the wall of the basal turn of the cochlea.
evidence: This describes a measurement procedure used in the study.

claim: Animals were anesthetized using intraperitoneally injected mixtures of ketamine (80 mg/kg) and xylazine (12 mg/kg).
source: Animals were anesthetized using intraperitoneally injected mixtures of ketamine (80 mg/kg) and xylazine (12 mg/kg).
evidence: This describes the anesthesia protocol.

claim: The theoretical resolution of the OCT system was ~3.5 µm across a 3.5 mm depth-of-field.
source: The theoretical resolution of the OCT system was ~3.5 µm across a 3.5 mm depth-of-field (i.e., z-range)
evidence: This describes a technical specification of the measurement system.

claim: The linear operating range of the OCT system was >500 µm.
source: The linear operating range of the OCT system was >500 µm.
evidence: This describes a technical specification of the measurement system.
